title: All the Anti-AI background noise. How do you deal?
author: couldgiveaflyingfck
selftext:
I absolutely love my Claude Ultra account. It's one of the few times in my life that I would genuinely be willing to walk 1,000 miles just to hand someone $200, and I'd do it enthusiastically.

For the first time in my life, I'm no longer just a passenger sitting in front of my high-end gaming PC. I'm in the driver's seat, directing it, putting it to work, and creating things I never imagined I'd be capable of building myself. The entire experience has been genuinely eye-opening, and even now, I find myself surprised by what I'm able to accomplish. I wake up every morning with my mind racing with ideas, possibilities, and things I want to create. The level of imagination, motivation, and sense of purpose this has brought into my life is something I honestly never expected.

I can build virtually any application or game I can imagine. Obviously, my lack of formal expertise in software development presents limitations, but that's part of the appeal. I'm pushing myself, learning new things, solving problems, and becoming more capable every single day. That's what excites me.

Case in point, here is a tool I am currently working on to give away for free to this community and others. It's a Claude MPC bridged tool that does imagination to prompt to 2D to 3D to 3D motion at nearly any level you need from it. From pixels to triple AAA titles. It can export to anything and in may different ways. Claude can directly pull from it the assets your game needs. You can export to 3D printers, Apple, and even the Amiga. This is a short demo that you might be interested in - [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KZpZec9zXGw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KZpZec9zXGw)

And that's exactly how I look at all the anti-AI background noise. In fact, I've applied this same philosophy to life for most of my adult years, going all the way back to when I was about 15 in 1984.

I see so many people here who seem genuinely bothered by those who dislike or oppose AI. But why? What are you getting out of giving those people your attention? Isn't that just another distraction? Emotional baggage that someone else handed you, or worse, that you willingly picked up?

Here's some advice that applies to just about everything in life. You're going to encounter countless people who don't share your views, values, interests, or perspective. You don't owe every one of them your attention, and you certainly don't need to give their opinions free rent in your head.

I've never been bothered by the anti-AI crowd. Why would I be? Their opinions don't contribute anything meaningful to my life, my work, or what I'm trying to accomplish. I simply filter out the noise and keep moving.

I see plenty of posts discussing the psychological effects of the anti-AI crowd on others. And I often wonder why people are giving these discussions so much attention in the first place. The people who stop to read, argue, and engage are sometimes doing nothing more than becoming spectators in someone else's mental meltdown.

Don't drink from a poisoned well. It won't make you stronger, smarter, or more informed. It'll just leave you carrying someone else's negativity, wasting your energy, and losing momentum on the things that actually matter.

Protect your attention. Choose your battles. Keep moving forward.

replies.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
replies.body:
Welcome! I'll spare you all the past fallout you've probably had to deal with and simply say welcome aboard.

AI can genuinely change your life in ways that are both practical and meaningful. At this point, your imagination is really the only limit.

One thing I've been doing is running my own personal AI assistant through a domain I own. Every day, an AI Sonnet sub-agent visits my website and updates it with information relevant to my life.

It tracks my spending and medications, finds local events and provides directions, searches for deals, gathers weekly sales ads, reminds me of appointments, and even reminds me about friends I haven't spoken with in a while.

It also monitors the internet for things I'm interested in, including niche stuff like vintage Amiga hardware and games. It gathers and filters the news I actually want to see, rather than feeding me an endless stream of things I don't care about.

I even built an Android app for my kids. With their permission and voluntary opt-in, it shares their location with me on a map on my website so I can check that everyone is safe. My daughter loves calling me to meet for lunch, and now she can see exactly where I am, get directions, and even find inexpensive gas along the way.

I have local weather, current conditions, the time, and extended forecasts all available at a glance.

Honestly, it does so much for me that it's become one of the most useful websites I've ever built. And yes, I'm a little biased. LOL.

This is just one example of what's possible when you stop thinking of AI as something you visit in a browser and start thinking of it as something you can build into your everyday life.

The possibilities are enormous.
